(CNN) -- Voters in Nashville, Tennessee -- a city that has seen a dramatic increase in its immigrant population -- rejected a measure Thursday that would have made English the only language used for government business in its metropolitan area. Nearly 57 percent of those who cast ballots Thursday in Nashville, Tennessee, voted against the measure. With all 173 precincts reporting, 41,752 voters, or nearly 57 percent, voted against the proposed amendment, with 32,144 voters supporting it, according to unofficial results posted on the Nashville city government Web site. "No person shall have a right to government services in any other language," the proposal read. The measure would have included government meetings. The Metropolitan Council, which submitted the measure, could have mandated exceptions to protect public health and safety. Elise Shore, southeast director of the Mexican-American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, said her regional office in Atlanta, Georgia, was monitoring the Nashville balloting. "We just elected our first black president. There are the forces of globalization and conducting business around the world ... in the face of this, we see these measures?" Shore asked. The proposal "sends a strong message ... this is a negative message. In fact, it invites discrimination," she said. In a newspaper editorial published Thursday, The Tennessean urged voters to defeat the proposal. "This amendment would exclude and marginalize those residents and visitors to Nashville simply because English is not their native tongue," the editorial said. The polls opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 7 p.m. Before the measure was defeated, a spokesman for U.S. English Inc., an action group that supports English-only laws nationwide, said the Nashville proposal was a good one. "Government programs are aimed at helping people reach self-sufficiency and success," Rob Toonkel said. "Allowing use of a second language doesn't encourage them to learn English." "The key word [of the amendment] is 'actions that bind the government,' " Toonkel said, which would cover transactions such as getting a city contract. If a non-English speaker needs help filling out a form, and someone in that agency speaks their language, they should be helped, he said. "But you shouldn't be able to come in, pick up a form [in another language] and leave." According to Toonkel, about 30 states and more than 100 localities have made English their official language, and he said his organization believes such laws are legal. Raul Gonzalez, legislative director for the National Council of La Raza, said the message of the proposal is discriminatory. "What it ... says is, 'If you speak a language other than English, you may not be welcome here,' " Gonzalez said. La Raza is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization focused on reducing poverty and discrimination and improving opportunities for Hispanic Americans. Gonzalez said similar English-only laws across the country "have so many exceptions they are meaningless." In an editorial earlier this month, The Tennessean quoted the referendum's sponsor, Councilman Eric Crafton, who said the bill was needed to save the city $100,000 to $150,000 in annual translation and related costs. However, metro officials told the newspaper such services are provided by employees already on the city's payroll. The council passed a similar bill in 2007, but it was vetoed by then-Mayor Bill Purcell, who called it "unconstitutional, unnecessary and mean-spirited," according to The Tennessean. U.S. Census data from 2000 showed an increase of 210 percent in the immigrant population of the Nashville metro area, including Davidson County, since 1990. During that decade, immigrants accounted for 45 percent of the overall population increase in the city. More than two-thirds, or 67 percent, of the area's foreign-born population had entered since 1990. This was much higher than the rate for the state overall, which was about 58 percent. The Census Bureau's American Community Survey, taken between 2005 and 2007 for the Nashville metro area, shows a population of 613,632. Of that number, 61,843 were foreign-born, with most of the immigrants coming from Latin America. About 73,000 residents speak a language other than English at home and, of those, 35,290 speak English less than "very well," the survey found.

# Nashville voters reject English-only government measure

**NASHVILLE, Tennessee (CNN)** — Voters in Nashville rejected a proposed charter amendment that would have required the metropolitan government to conduct most official business in English.

The measure, known as “English First,” was defeated Thursday, with about 57% voting against it and 43% supporting it, according to unofficial election results.

The proposal would have required government communications, publications and services to be provided in English, with exceptions for public health and safety, emergencies, court proceedings and services mandated by federal law.

Supporters argued that a common language would promote unity and reduce the cost of translation. Critics said the amendment was unnecessary and could discourage immigrants from seeking police protection, medical assistance and other essential services.

Nashville Mayor Karl Dean opposed the measure, as did business, religious and civil rights groups. Opponents also warned that adopting an English-only policy could damage the city’s reputation as an increasingly diverse and welcoming community.

The referendum was championed by former Metro Council member Eric Crafton, who said local government should not be required to provide services in multiple languages.

Nashville’s immigrant population has grown significantly in recent decades, bringing new communities from Latin America, Asia, Africa and the Middle East. The city is also home to one of the nation’s largest Kurdish populations.

The vote drew attention beyond Tennessee as communities across the country debated how local governments should respond to increasing linguistic diversity. Nashville would have become one of the largest U.S. cities to impose an English-only requirement on municipal business.

A separate proposal on the ballot, intended to prevent the government from discriminating against or favoring residents based on language, also failed.

counterfactuals.output:
## Nashville voters reject English-only measure

On January 22, 2009, voters in Nashville–Davidson County defeated a proposed Metro Charter amendment that would have required most city-government business and communications to be conducted in English.

- **Against:** 41,752 votes — **56.5%**
- **For:** 32,144 votes — **43.5%**
- **Total votes:** 73,896  
- Turnout was roughly **15% of registered voters** in the special election.

### Reactions

Councilman **Eric Crafton**, the principal sponsor, argued that an English-first policy would encourage assimilation, promote a common civic language and prevent local government from routinely expanding translation services. After the defeat, he acknowledged the result but said the campaign had at least focused attention on the role of English.

Opponents—including Mayor **Karl Dean**, business groups, religious leaders, immigrant advocates and the **Nashville for All of Us** coalition—celebrated the vote as evidence that Nashville wanted to remain welcoming to immigrants and international businesses. Dean said voters had sent a clear message about the kind of community they wanted Nashville to be.

Critics had also warned that the amendment was ambiguously written, could interfere with police, emergency, health and other public services, and might expose Metro government to litigation or loss of federal funds. Supporters maintained that federally required services and genuine health-and-safety emergencies would have been exempt.

### What the proposal would have done

The amendment would have declared English the official language of Nashville’s metropolitan government and generally prohibited Metro agencies and employees from conducting government business or issuing communications in other languages, except where federal law or public-health and safety needs required otherwise.

Although often described simply as an “English-only” initiative, supporters preferred the term **“English First.”**

### History of the proposal

Crafton had pursued the policy for several years:

1. He first advanced an English-language ordinance through the Metro Council.
2. In early 2007, then-Mayor **Bill Purcell** vetoed the legislation, and the council did not override him.
3. Crafton and his allies then used a petition drive to place a charter amendment before voters.
4. After disputes over petition signatures and election procedures, the question was scheduled for the January 2009 countywide special election.
5. A heavily organized opposition campaign, backed by civic, business, religious and immigrant groups, ultimately defeated it.

The special election itself cost Metro government several hundred thousand dollars, which opponents cited as another objection.

### Nashville’s immigration context

The campaign occurred after unusually rapid immigration-driven growth:

- Contemporary Census estimates indicated that roughly **one in ten Davidson County residents was foreign-born**, amounting to approximately **60,000–70,000 people**, depending on the estimate and year used.
- Nashville’s foreign-born population had grown severalfold since 1990; studies commonly identified the metropolitan area as one of the nation’s fastest-growing immigrant destinations during the 1990s and early 2000s.
- The city had substantial Kurdish, Hispanic, Somali, Vietnamese and other immigrant communities. Nashville was frequently described as having the largest Kurdish population in the United States.
- Immigrants were an important part of the local construction, hospitality, health-care and service-sector workforce.

Those demographic changes shaped both sides’ arguments: supporters portrayed the measure as a way to preserve a shared language during rapid change, while opponents said it would stigmatize newcomers and damage Nashville’s reputation as an internationally oriented city.

**Nashville voters reject official-English amendment as broad coalition warns of economic and social costs**

**NASHVILLE, Tenn. —** Nearly 57 percent of Nashville voters rejected a proposed charter amendment that would have made English the official language of the metropolitan government, delivering a decisive defeat to a measure critics said would isolate immigrants, damage the city’s reputation and create unnecessary legal and administrative problems.

The proposal, voted down in a January 2009 special election, would have required most Metro Nashville government business and communications to be conducted in English. It included exceptions in areas such as public health and safety and where federal law required language assistance, but opponents argued that the wording was still broad enough to discourage city agencies from communicating effectively with residents who had limited English proficiency.

The result—roughly 57 percent against and 43 percent in favor—reflected the strength of an unusually wide opposition coalition. Immigrant-rights organizations joined business leaders, religious congregations, civil-liberties advocates, educators and elected officials, including then-Mayor Karl Dean, in campaigning against the amendment.

Because there was no comprehensive exit polling, it is impossible to assign a single motive to the majority that voted “no.” But the campaign highlighted several factors that appear to have shaped the result.

### Concern about Nashville’s welcoming image

Opponents framed the amendment not simply as a rule governing city paperwork but as a public statement about who belonged in Nashville.

The city had experienced rapid demographic change, with growing Latino, Kurdish, Somali and other immigrant and refugee communities. Advocacy groups warned that declaring English the only language for most official activity could make those residents less likely to seek help from police, health departments, schools and other public agencies.

The opposition campaign emphasized that many immigrants were learning English and that rejecting the amendment did not amount to rejecting English as a shared language. Instead, organizers argued, the question was whether local government should retain the flexibility to communicate with residents when safety, access to services or effective administration required it.

That message allowed voters to support English as the country’s dominant language while still opposing a legal restriction on government communication.

### Business leaders warned of economic damage

Nashville’s business community also played a prominent role in defeating the proposal. Employers and economic-development advocates said the amendment could undercut the city’s effort to present itself as an open, internationally connected place to live, work and invest.

At the time, Nashville was seeking corporate investment, international tourism and a larger role in the global economy. Critics said the official-English label could generate national publicity suggesting that the city was hostile to immigrants and foreign-born professionals.

The Nashville Area Chamber of Commerce and other business voices argued that the potential reputational cost outweighed any symbolic benefit. Their participation broadened the campaign beyond traditional immigrant-rights constituencies and gave fiscally conservative or business-oriented voters a reason to oppose the measure.

### Questions about cost, legality and necessity

Opponents also challenged the amendment on practical grounds.

Federal civil-rights laws and funding requirements can obligate government agencies to provide meaningful access to people with limited English proficiency. The proposed charter change could not override those federal responsibilities. As a result, critics said the measure might produce confusion over when translation was allowed, while doing little to reduce the services the city was legally required to provide.

Civil-liberties organizations raised the possibility of litigation over the amendment’s meaning and application. City departments, they argued, could face added legal review and administrative expense as officials tried to determine whether particular translations, notices or multilingual outreach efforts were permitted.

Critics further noted that English was already the routine language of Metro government. The amendment therefore appeared to many voters to offer few concrete administrative benefits. Opponents portrayed it as a solution to a problem that had not been demonstrated.

The cost of holding a special election also became part of the debate, reinforcing the argument that the proposal was an unnecessary diversion from more pressing municipal concerns.

### A coordinated grassroots campaign

The umbrella organization **Nashville for All of Us** became the public face of the opposition. Its campaign brought together immigrant and refugee advocates, clergy, neighborhood organizers, educators, business groups and civil-rights organizations.

Volunteers conducted voter outreach, held community meetings and used phone banks and door-to-door canvassing to argue that the amendment would affect the entire city, not just residents who spoke languages other than English. Faith leaders addressed the issue as one of hospitality and human dignity, while immigrant organizations focused on the practical need for residents to communicate with emergency responders and public agencies.

The **Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition** and allied groups treated the result as evidence that an organized local campaign could overcome a measure built around concerns about immigration and cultural change. They praised Nashville voters for choosing inclusion and said the vote showed that immigrant communities could build effective alliances with established civic institutions.

Civil-liberties advocates similarly welcomed the defeat, saying governments should not impose language restrictions that could interfere with public access or free expression. Business organizations emphasized a different but complementary message: Nashville had protected its reputation as a growing, welcoming city.

National organizations on both sides closely watched the election. Supporters of official-English policies had viewed Nashville as an important test case for passing such a requirement at the municipal level. After the defeat, English-only advocates maintained that government should promote a common language and argued that the proposal had been mischaracterized. The amendment’s leading local supporter, Metro Council member Eric Crafton, had said it was intended to encourage assimilation and prevent government from being expected to operate in numerous languages.

Opponents countered that English acquisition and language access were not mutually exclusive. A resident could be learning English, they said, and still need immediate help understanding a police warning, health notice or government form.

### A vote with national significance

The Nashville result drew attention beyond Tennessee because official-English measures had succeeded in a number of states and localities. Nashville’s rejection demonstrated that such proposals could be defeated when opponents combined humanitarian concerns with arguments about public safety, government efficiency and economic competitiveness.

For advocacy groups, the most important lesson was the breadth of the coalition. Immigrant-rights organizers did not campaign alone; they were joined by institutions with substantial influence among longtime Nashville voters.

The nearly 57 percent “no” vote therefore represented more than a reaction to the amendment’s technical language. It reflected concerns about whether the measure was needed, whether it could be enforced without legal complications, and what message it would send about a city increasingly shaped by immigration and international ties.

In the aftermath, opponents described the result as an affirmation that Nashville could maintain English as its common civic language without limiting the government’s ability to communicate with all of its residents.

# Nashville Voters Rejected an “English-Only” Government in 2009

On January 22, 2009, Nashville voters rejected a proposed charter amendment that would have restricted the metropolitan government’s use of languages other than English. The special-election referendum, promoted by Metro Council member Eric Crafton, drew national attention and became a test of how a rapidly diversifying Southern city would respond to demands for an official-government-language policy.

The proposal would have declared English the language of Nashville’s metropolitan government and generally prohibited agencies from providing services in other languages unless federal law required them. Crafton argued that the measure would encourage immigrants to learn English, reduce translation expenses and give voters control over the government’s language policies. Critics countered that it could impede communication involving public safety, health, courts and other essential services while damaging Nashville’s reputation as a welcoming city.

Voters defeated the amendment by roughly 57 percent to 43 percent. A companion proposal intended to make future charter amendments more difficult to place on the ballot also failed.

## A locally framed campaign with national participants

Crafton’s campaign received support from U.S. English Inc., a national organization that advocates making English the official language of government. The organization supplied financial and strategic assistance and presented the referendum as part of a broader effort to promote a common civic language.

Opponents organized under the banner Nashville for All of Us, a coalition that included business executives, religious leaders, immigrant advocates and community organizations. National civil-rights groups also entered the debate. The National Council of La Raza—now known as UnidosUS—and the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, or MALDEF, opposed the proposal, arguing that it would burden immigrant communities and could expose the city to legal disputes over access to government programs.

The presence of U.S. English, La Raza and MALDEF allowed each side to accuse the other of relying on outside interests. Yet the campaign’s outcome was also shaped by local institutions. Nashville’s hospitality and health-care industries, churches, civil-rights organizations and many elected officials warned that the amendment could undermine economic development and public safety.

## *The Tennessean* urged a “no” vote

Nashville’s daily newspaper, *The Tennessean*, opposed the English-only amendment. Its editorial position emphasized that English already was the ordinary language of Metro government and that officials still needed flexibility to communicate with residents in emergencies and in the delivery of public services.

The newspaper also argued that the proposal sent an unnecessarily hostile message at a time when Nashville was trying to attract international businesses, workers and visitors. Like many opponents, its editorial board treated the referendum not simply as a question about translation costs, but as a decision about the city’s identity and economic ambitions.

## What the Census showed

Census figures provided important context for the controversy. Around the time of the vote, Census Bureau surveys showed that English remained overwhelmingly dominant in Davidson County, but that linguistic diversity had grown substantially during the preceding decade. Roughly one resident in six age five or older spoke a language other than English at home, according to American Community Survey estimates from the period. Spanish was the largest non-English language category.

The same data also showed why the phrase “non-English-speaking” could be misleading. Many people who spoke another language at home reported that they also spoke English well or very well. A smaller share—roughly 6 percent of residents age five or older in estimates from the late 2000s—reported speaking English less than “very well.” Census tables measure language use and self-reported proficiency; they do not establish that everyone in that category requires government translation for every interaction.

Nashville’s demographic changes were nevertheless striking. Immigration and refugee resettlement had increased the city’s Latino, Kurdish, Somali and other international communities. Those trends created practical demands for interpretation in schools, hospitals, emergency response and public-information campaigns, even though most government business continued to be conducted in English.

## The referendum’s meaning

The vote did not make English less central to Nashville government. Rather, it preserved the metropolitan government’s discretion to use other languages when officials considered that useful or necessary.

Crafton and U.S. English portrayed the proposal as a measure for civic unity and governmental efficiency. La Raza, MALDEF and local opponents viewed it as a threat to equal access and to Nashville’s growing international profile. *The Tennessean* sided with the latter view, arguing that the amendment offered few practical benefits and significant symbolic and administrative costs.

In rejecting the measure, Nashville voters chose flexibility over a charter-level restriction. The result became a notable episode in the national debate over official-English laws—and a sign that the city’s changing demographics had begun to reshape its politics as well as its neighborhoods.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a neutral, fact-based CNN report on Nashville’s defeated English-only proposal, quoting both sides of the debate and providing context about translation costs and the city’s growing immigrant population.
counterfactuals.output:
**Nashville voters reject English-only proposal**

**NASHVILLE, Tennessee (CNN)** — Nashville voters rejected a proposal that would have required most city government business to be conducted in English, ending a campaign that drew national attention to the city’s rapidly changing population.

The charter amendment was defeated by roughly 57% to 43% in a January 2009 special election.

The measure would have required Nashville’s metropolitan government to communicate in English except when other languages were mandated by state or federal law or needed to protect public health and safety. It also would have restricted government employees’ use of other languages while performing official duties.

Councilman Eric Crafton, who led the campaign for the amendment, argued that a common language would promote unity and reduce government spending.

“This is not about immigration. This is about language,” Crafton said during the campaign. He estimated that the city spent about $100,000 a year on translation and interpretation services, although city officials said a precise total was difficult to calculate because the expenses were spread among departments.

Opponents, organized under the banner Nashville for All of Us, said the proposal could make it harder for residents with limited English skills to report crimes, obtain medical help or access basic city services. They also warned that enforcing the amendment and defending it in court could cost more than the translation services supporters criticized.

Mayor Karl Dean, who opposed the measure, said after the vote that the result showed Nashville was “a welcoming city.”

The debate reflected Nashville’s demographic transformation. Census figures showed that the number of foreign-born residents increased sharply during the 1990s and continued to grow in the following decade. The city became home to expanding Latino, Kurdish, Somali and Southeast Asian communities; Nashville is widely described as having one of the largest Kurdish populations in the United States.

Supporters said immigrants should learn English and that government should not be expected to provide routine services in multiple languages. Opponents agreed that English proficiency was important but said translation can be essential in emergencies and can help newcomers participate in civic life while they learn the language.

The vote did not make another language official or require Nashville to provide translations in every circumstance. It left existing practices in place, allowing individual agencies to offer interpretation or translated materials when officials consider them necessary or when the law requires them.
